content.p: The Mongrel Mob is one of New Zealand's best-known street gangs, with roots in the 1960s. CNN describes its members as mostly Māori. Its history cannot be told without two other things: a generation of children raised in state institutions, and a long run of confrontations with police, courts and rival gangs. In November 2024 a new law banned the public display of gang insignia, and within three minutes of its taking effect a Mongrel Mob member had been charged under it.

This account covers where the gang came from, what former members told a royal commission about the boys' homes behind it, how the police and the courts have dealt with it, and the violence that keeps it in the news.
content.h2: A name from a courtroom, and a start in care
content.p: The gang's own story of its name goes like this. Some time in the 1960s a group of young offenders stood before a judge in Hastings, a Hawke's Bay city of about 49,000 people. The judge, berating them, called them "nothing but a pack of mongrels". A catalogue entry on the DigitalNZ aggregator introduces it as "the legend", and the entry cites no court record for it.

A firmer thread runs through state welfare. Dr Jarrod Gilbert is a University of Canterbury senior lecturer who wrote Patched, a history of the country's gangs. He told the Otago Daily Times in 2022 that the gang's roots lie in boys' homes, among them Epuni in Lower Hutt and the Kohitere training centre in Levin. "It's directly where they formed," he said, "so the history between problems in state care and the Mongrel Mob is intrinsically intertwined."

CNN's later account puts the gangs in a wider setting. Outlaw motorcycle clubs and patched street gangs spread through New Zealand from the 1960s, it said, a period when Māori were being drawn away from their ancestral homes into cities and Polynesian migrants who had come for work and education faced an immigration crackdown. Gangs offered fraternity, status and protection to marginalised people.

The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care heard from former gang members about those institutions. Two men gave evidence at its Māori hearings, and the New Zealand Herald reported their accounts in March 2022.

Paora Sweeney became a ward of the state as a boy after the deaths of his parents and a sister. He said he was hit in the mouth by a housemaster on his first day in a boys' home in Kirikiroa and then moved through homes at Hokio Beach and Kohitere. Inside, he said, housemasters and other boys used heavy violence, and the system worked something like a gang. At Kohitere, he said, the boys were split between two villas, one affiliated with the Mongrel Mob and one with Black Power. After a fight that housemasters had sanctioned, in which he cracked another boy's skull, he said he emerged from a secure unit with a new standing among the boys. He earned his first patch at 15, he said, and later started the Hamilton chapter of the Mongrel Mob. The Herald reported that he was also convicted and served time as a party to a gang rape. The Herald said he has now lived 31 years free of gang life and addictions.

Wiremu Waikari told the commission he was beaten by a housemaster on his first night at Epuni at the age of 10. He described no schooling there, just daily violence and "slave labour". He later joined the Mongrel Mob and now works as a social worker. He told the commission that he believed the growth of gangs in the 1970s and 1980s was a direct result of how young Māori had been treated by the Crown years earlier.

Journalist Aaron Smale, writing for 1News on the day the commission's final report was made public in July 2024, described a submission from gang members to the commission. He said it showed that gang members had often entered state care for trivial reasons and then spent years suffering violence and often sexual abuse. He wrote that by the 1970s Māori made up 70 to 80 percent of the residents in some institutions.

The gangs have begun to look inward. In August 2022 the Waikato chapter, known as the Mongrel Mob Kingdom, ran a weekend hui at Poihākena Marae in Raglan on trauma and abuse in care, thought to be a New Zealand first. A former Lake Alice patient, Paul Zentveld, spoke to a room of members and families, and three staff from the royal commission attended to listen. Kingdom spokesperson Louise Hutchinson said that amid public talk of gangs as the cause of crime, "the gangs have their own story to tell". Gilbert said gangs have historically rejected state agencies, so it was hard to win their trust, even for an independent inquiry.

Gang violence in Hawke's Bay and Tairāwhiti has drawn repeated police attention. In April 2025 Eastern District Police obtained a Gang Conflict Warrant over what it called "ongoing tensions" between the Mongrel Mob and Black Power in Tairāwhiti and Hawke's Bay. The warrant allowed officers to search the vehicles of suspected gang members and to seize firearms, weapons and vehicles. It followed a night in Wairoa when, police said, shots were fired at houses belonging to members of both gangs, and a house in Napier was also targeted. Two men, aged 18 and 35, were arrested over the Wairoa shootings. Detective Inspector Marty James said there had been other incidents, including assaults and vehicle rammings, that had not been reported to police.

Wairoa's mayor, Craig Little, told CNN he estimated that 80 percent of the town's crime was related to gangs. Bronson Edwards, a Mongrel Mob chapter captain there, said conflict between the two gangs was still going on because "some people still needed to learn some lessons".

The violence reaches into prisons. In June 2022 an inmate said by the Herald to be a Mongrel Mob member stabbed a Corrections officer 12 times in the face with an improvised metal weapon at Hawke's Bay Regional Prison. The officer was discharged from hospital that night and was expected to make a full recovery, said the Corrections Association president. The prisoner had been held under directed segregation and was due to be moved the next day.

Violence against the public also appears in the courts. In March 2025 Jayden Kennedy, 28, a patched Mongrel Mob member, was jailed for five years and eight months in the Rotorua District Court for kidnapping, blackmail and assault. Judge Greg Hollister-Jones said Kennedy had held a woman under 20, visiting from Hawke's Bay, in a car for about four hours after she asked for help, and told her "You bleed red now", a reference, the judge said, to his patched status. She was made to withdraw $120 from a cash machine. The judge said Kennedy also sexually assaulted her and she was threatened with a welding hammer. Police found the car; it sped off and crashed into another car, and Kennedy later parked and allowed her to escape. Two alleged associates denied charges over the offending.

New Zealand's coalition government brought in the insignia ban in response to growing public concern about gangs, CNN reported. The Gangs Act 2024, with dispersal and non-consorting powers, took effect at midnight on 21 November 2024. People caught displaying insignia in public faced a fine of up to NZ$5,000 or up to six months in prison.

At 12:03 a.m. police stopped a car in Hastings. They said it carried a large Mongrel Mob sign on the dashboard, and the driver, a 51-year-old Napier man who was not wearing a patch, was summonsed to appear in court. Police Minister Mark Mitchell said he believed gang members, whom he believed to be from the Mongrel Mob, had come out to test the law. Labour's deputy leader, Carmel Sepuloni, called the ban "theatrics" that would not address why people join gangs.

In Tauranga that month, police monitored the tangi of Wayne Kelly, a prominent Mongrel Mob member, and his partner. Three men, Brandon Fowler, Manaia Kimura and Dion Haitana, pleaded not guilty to displaying Mongrel Mob insignia on a T-shirt, a bulldog insignia and rings respectively, in public. A fourth man, Jose Manuel Waenga, was charged over the number 13, and pleaded guilty to that and four other charges.

The ban's first year produced contested results. CNN reported that police seized 192 patches in the first 12 months, that more than 850 charges had been laid for breaches, and that 22 people were jailed in the first six months. The government counted a 23 percent fall in victims of violent offending between October 2024 and August 2025 as a win, though CNN noted the justice ministry's survey data does not say which offending is gang-related. Acting Assistant Commissioner Corrie Parnell conceded that it was hard to draw a link between seizing patches and changes in drug crime. The national gang list had grown by more than 700 in the year, to 10,242 people in November 2025. Edwards, the Mongrel Mob chapter captain, told CNN the gangs were "just less visible" and that numbers in his chapter "have grown".

The courts have not always sided with police on what to do with seized patches. In September 2025 Judge Bruce Davidson ordered police to return the patch of Syd Te Rata, a 40-year-old member of the Mongrel Mob Notorious chapter, who had been stopped on his motorcycle in Lower Hutt at about 3:30 a.m. on 19 April 2025. He had ridden home wearing it after visiting the house of a friend who had died, and said he wore it to feel close to the man. In July he had been convicted and discharged for displaying insignia, and sentenced to community detention and supervision for refusing a blood test.

His lawyer argued that the patch was akin to a "family crest", as his father, uncles and grandfather had all been patched members. The judge accepted that the law gave courts wide discretion over forfeited regalia, and that the words "otherwise dispose of" were wide enough to allow its return. There was "no public disorder", he said, "no threats, no violence".

It was the second time in two months that a court had ordered a patch returned. Mitchell said he was "disappointed, without a doubt", while adding that he does not comment on judicial decisions. He said police would appeal and that he would seek advice on whether the law needed to change. Newsroom reported that the justice minister, Paul Goldsmith, said more than 200 people had been convicted and a third of them had their insignia seized, and that the ban was working "very well". Labour's Duncan Webb said a minister should leave judges alone to do their job.

The gang members' own line is that a patch is not the same as the crime. "Serious crime has never been done with a patch on," Edwards said. Police told CNN that the ban allowed communities to feel safer, and that they use both overt and covert methods, including photographs taken at funerals, to collect evidence.
